#FunFact: In the 1990s, CERN released the World Wide Web into the public domain. On April 30, 1993, CERN issued a statement making the Web software available on a royalty-free basis, making the web accessible to everyone.

Curious about CERN’s history? Explore more in our achives: https://sis.web.cern.ch/archives | CERN

excerpts.text:
Today is especially important in the history of the web since on April 30, 1993, [CERN](http://public.web.cern.ch/public/), the European Organization for Nuclear Research, released World Wide Web into the public domain.

In the document making the release official, W. Hoogland, Director of Research, and H. Weber, Director of Administration, referred to World Wide Web, or W3 for short, as “a global computer networked information system.” It further stated that “CERN’s intention in this is to further compatibility, common practices, and standards in networking and computer supported collaboration.” ([page 1](http://www.w3.org/History/1993/CERN/page1.png), [page 2](http://www.w3.org/History/1993/CERN/page2.png))

excerpts.text:
On 30 April 1993 CERN issued a public statement stating that the three components of Web software (the basic line-mode client, the basic server and the library of common code) were put in the Public Domain with the statement:

CERN relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code, both source and binary and permission is given to anyone to use, duplicate, modify and distribute it.

assessment.rationale: The 30 April 1993 public domain statement is corroborated by the contextual note that free/open software concepts were in their infancy in the early 1990s, supporting the assertion's factual basis.
limitations: Contextual remark does not quantify the scope of royalty-free reuse

excerpts.text: On April 30, 1993, CERN made a landmark decision that changed computing forever.
**Correct Answer:** The World Wide Web software and protocols, released royalty-free into the public domain

On April 30, 1993, CERN released the core World Wide Web software, including HTTP, HTML, and the original web server and browser code (WorldWideWeb/Nexus), into the public domain, royalty-free. This was a deliberate and historic decision by CERN management, largely championed by Tim Berners-Lee, who had originally proposed the Web in 1989.

excerpts.text: Tim Berners-Lee wrote the [first proposal for the World Wide Web](http://cds.cern.ch/record/369245/files/ARCH-WWW-4-010.pdf) in March 1989.
The document described a “hypertext project” called “WorldWideWeb” in which a “web” of “hypertext documents” could be viewed by “browsers”.
In 1991, Berners-Lee released his WWW software.

A few months later, in August 1991, he [announced the WWW software on Internet newsgroups](https://www.w3.org/People/Berners-Lee/1991/08/art-6484.txt) and interest in the project spread around the world.
On 30 April 1993, CERN made the source code of WorldWideWeb available on a royalty-free basis, making it free software.
